analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose workplace surveillance of workers and bans some of it outright.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 6 Senate sponsors but never got a hearing or a vote, dying in committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Stop Spying Bosses Act would require employers with 11 or more workers to tell workers exactly what data is collected about them, how it is used, and how it feeds into hiring, firing, and performance decisions. It would ban several surveillance practices outright — including spying on union activity, monitoring workers off the clock or in sensitive areas, collecting health information unrelated to the job, and selling worker data. It would also create a new Privacy and Technology Division inside the Department of Labor to enforce the rules, and give workers the right to sue over violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at covered employers, who would gain the right to know what their employers track about them, review that data, correct errors, and sue when employers cross the lines the bill draws. Labor organizations would also gain, since the bill would bar employers from using surveillance to identify or monitor union organizing.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must disclose any workplace surveillance to workers and applicants, including what data is collected, how and when it is collected, how it is used, and how it affects performance assessments [S2][S3].

Employers may not use surveillance to identify or monitor workers' union organizing or other protected concerted activity, may not monitor workers off-duty or in sensitive areas like restrooms and lactation rooms, and may not collect health or immigration information unrelated to the job [S2][S3].

Employers cannot sell or license worker data collected through surveillance, must get consent before transferring personal data to third parties, and must tell workers within 7 days when a hiring, firing, or promotion decision relied on surveillance data, letting them review and correct it [S3].

The bill creates a Privacy and Technology Division in the Department of Labor to write and enforce the rules, protects workers from retaliation for complaining, and gives workers and unions a private right to sue with statutory damages up to $20,000 per violation of the surveillance prohibitions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers, including government employers, bear the compliance costs: documenting and disclosing every surveillance practice, responding to worker data requests, and restricting how they collect and share data. Workplace surveillance and HR technology vendors lose a market for products the bill prohibits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers and surveillance tech vendors

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on all covered employers, including small firms with as few as 11 workers, which must document and disclose every monitoring practice and respond to worker data requests within tight deadlines [S3].

The bill's definitions are broad — 'data' sweeps in productivity information, emails, device usage, and even off-duty social media — so routine management and security tools could fall under the disclosure and prohibition rules, raising legal risk for ordinary business practices [S3].

The private right of action carries statutory damages up to $20,000 per violation (up to $40,000 for willful or repeated ones) and overrides pre-dispute arbitration agreements for claims under the bill, which opponents would argue invites litigation against employers [S3].
A ban on collecting data not 'reasonably related to operations' could complicate legitimate workplace safety, security, and investigations that employers and even workers may want [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and specific: workers would finally know what their bosses track, and the most intrusive practices — union spying, off-duty monitoring, selling worker data — would be illegal. The costs are compliance burdens and litigation exposure that scale with how broadly regulators and courts read the bill's broad definitions. A bill this ambitious could have been narrowed (for example, by raising the employer threshold or capping damages) without losing much protection, but as introduced the privacy gains clearly outweigh the costs for the workers it covers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by original cosponsors Booker, Schatz, Fetterman, and Warren — all Senate Democrats or independents [S1][S5].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that referral is the last action recorded in its entire history [S5].
The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote in either chamber during the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and workplace-surveillance technology vendors are better off: they face no federal requirement to disclose what they track about workers, and practices the bill would have banned — union surveillance, off-duty monitoring, selling worker data — remain lawful absent other law. Workers gained nothing. Because the bill received no action beyond a referral, no recorded opposition appears in the record; the outcome was determined by the committee's decision not to schedule it.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey

for.name: Sens. Booker, Schatz, Fetterman, and Warren
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, joining as independents where applicable; no other senators joined afterward.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; no action followed its February 2023 referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; all six sponsors were Democrats or independents, and no Republican cosponsor joined [S4].

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and HR technology vendors
industries.note: Firms selling productivity monitoring, biometric, and automated decision systems would face new disclosure duties, outright bans on key products and uses, and liability for violations. Their revenue from worker monitoring runs directly against the privacy the bill guarantees workers [S3].

Employers would bear real compliance costs — disclosures, data requests, and litigation exposure — but would also gain clearer rules and cannot sell worker data under the bill. As a group they opposed the added regulation by declining to support it, though the record shows no formal opposition [S3][S4].
The bill bans selling or licensing worker data and requires consent and encryption before any third-party transfer, cutting off a market for employee data [S3].
Unions would gain both a prohibition on employer surveillance of organizing activity and standing to sue violators themselves [S3].
